# Draft:German Archaeological Institute at Rome

The Rome Department of the German Archaeological Institute (, ) is the oldest archaeological research institution in Rome and is considered one of the birthplaces of scientific archaeology. Today, the institute is a department of the German Archaeological Institute (DAI), which developed out of the Instituto di corrispondenza archeologica in Rome. The DAI is a public institution funded by the German state, headquartered in Berlin and operating under the jurisdiction of the Federal Foreign Office.
The Rome Department maintains a library of classical studies of global importance, one of the largest specialized photographic collections on Italian archaeology, and a wealth of resources for scholarly work, including extensive archives and a digital catalog for rapid access to publications.The DAI Rome focuses on the archaeology of Italy and North Africa, from prehistoric times to the early Middle Ages. The current director is Ortwin Dally, with Norbert Zimmermann serving as deputy director.
History and purpose
The Instituto di corrispondenza archeologica was founded on April 21, 1829, on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, in the Palazzo Caffarelli, as a private association of international scholars and artists of classical antiquity. Its initial purpose was to collect and publish the rapidly increasing archaeological discoveries in Italy.  In regular assemblies of members and interested guests, called Adunanze, new finds were presented and discussed, and the methods of the emerging disciplines of classical scholarship were refined. A collection of exemplary artifacts and drawings of antiquities was also created. Particularly important for scholarship was the establishment of a comprehensive library, which remains a core component of the institute today. Since 1835, the Casa Tarpea—designed by Johann Michael Knapp—served as the institute's headquarters.
Strongly supported by the Prussian kings, the institute was converted in 1871 into an institution of the German Empire. In 1877, the now Imperial German Archaeological Institute moved into a new building on the Capitoline Hill, designed by Paul Laspeyres in Neo-Pompeian style, providing ample space for the expanding library. From that time onward, the institute undertook fruitful excavations at major Italian sites, such as Pompeii, Rome, and southern Italy, many of which it continues to study today. Numerous individual investigations of major monuments in Rome and Latium, as well as cataloging work, characterize the institute's scientific activity.
After the confiscation of the Capitoline building following World War I, the institute resumed work in 1924 in the parish house of the Christuskirche, at Via Sardegna 79, where it remains located.  In 1944, it was closed due to World War II, and from 1946, it came under the administration of the Unione internazionale degli istituti di archeologia, storia e storia dell’arte in Roma. The DAI was reestablished as a German institution in the summer of 1953, and a new purpose-built facility was completed at Via Sardegna in 1964. In addition to its traditional art-archaeological studies—central to German classical archaeology—focusing on the major collections in Rome, the institute today emphasizes historical-topographical, urbanistic, and architectural research questions. These complex studies increasingly require interdisciplinary cooperation and are often carried out in close collaboration with Italian institutions, and sometimes internationally. German universities are also actively involved. Thus, the institute not only fulfills its own research mission but also serves as a bridge between German academic research and Italian institutions. Moreover, the DAI Rome is dedicated to preserving, restoring, and documenting archaeological sites and monuments, recognizing the shared cultural heritage of all nations. In recent decades, its projects have expanded to nearly all of Italy, as well as Tunisia, Algeria, and Albania.
The institute also promotes international scholarly exchange through numerous lectures and colloquia, often held jointly with Italian and other Roman institutions. As a foreign organization, it serves as an ideal forum for academic collaboration. Two major annual celebrations are the Palilia Day on April 21 and the Winckelmann Festival on December 9, the birthday of Johann Joachim Winckelmann. These events are open to the public, while more specialized gatherings are aimed at the international scholarly community. A traditional highlight of the institute's outreach is the annual “Pompeii Course”, organized by its scholars for German high school teachers of classical languages and history, offering them an opportunity to deepen their knowledge of Roman antiquity through a particularly suitable example. The strong demand underscores its importance. Equally popular are the academic seminars and spring guided tours (January–May) conducted by institute members through Rome's monuments and museums.
As an institution funded by the Federal Republic of Germany, the DAI Rome operates under the Federal Foreign Office. However, most research projects are made possible through external funding organizations, such as the German Research Foundation (DFG), the Gerda Henkel Foundation, or the Fritz Thyssen Foundation.The building on Via Sardegna—currently closed for extensive renovations—houses not only the institute's core facilities but also a guest wing for visiting scholars. Equally important is the dependence “Villino Amelung” at Via Andrea Cesalpino 1b, a villa built in 1904 by Ernst Wille for the private scholar Walther Amelung (1865–1927). This villa provides temporary accommodation for research fellows and young scholars, including recipients of the DAI's travel grant, allowing them to work flexibly on-site and participate in ongoing research projects.
Current state
Due to structural deficiencies affecting the building's stability, the premises of the DAI Rome at Via Sardegna were closed to the public in 2006.  In autumn 2009, the institute moved into temporary quarters at Via Curtatone 4d, where the library and photographic archive were reopened to the public on January 26, 2010.In 2015, the institute relocated to another temporary building at Via Valadier 37. The original building at Via Sardegna 79 is currently under renovation and is expected to be returned to the DAI in a few years. In January 2019, the institute had to change locations once again; since June 2019, the Rome Department has been accessible at Via Sicilia 136.

Library
When the institute and its library were returned after the First World War, it was decreed that the library should never be removed from Rome, but it was nevertheless taken to the , the biggest Nazi-era bunker for stolen art, in early 1944. There it was found by Allied troops and transported back to Rome in early February 1946. From December 1947, the library was once again accessible in Via Sardegna. When, after interim administration by the Unione internazionale degli istituti di archeologia, storia e storia dell'arte in Roma, an agreement was reached in 1953 between the three Western Allies, Italy and the Federal Republic of Germany in 1953, it was agreed that the library should not be removed from Italy and that it should be open to scholars of all nations without restriction as a centre of international research.
Today, the library has over 220,000 volumes and collects literature on classical archaeology in the Mediterranean countries and neighbouring regions, i.e. on the ancient history of the Greco-Roman cultural sphere from the Aegean Bronze Age to the end of the seventh century AD. Works on classical philology and epigraphy as well as ancient history are also acquired, and titles on provincial Roman archaeology, prehistory and early history, Egyptology and Near Eastern archaeology are added. Currently, well over 2,000 monographs are acquired each year and the number of current journals amounts to around 1,200. The collection is recorded in the ZENON library catalogue and can be consulted.
The reading room in the institute's current premises in Via Sicilia has 64 seats. In principle, the library is open to researchers from all countries, but for practical reasons access for students is restricted, as the institute, as a research institution, deliberately targets a qualified specialist audience. For reasons of space, only some of the books are located in Via Sicilia; the other volumes are stored in a repository outside the city, but can be ordered to the reading room within a day.

The photo library
The photo library was established in the late 1920s under Ludwig Curtius in response to the need for a suitable working tool that would meet the growing importance of photographs for the formal analysis of archaeological objects. The collection currently comprises around 300,000 photographs, of which around 200,000 negatives are available. The collection is organised according to the main types of material within classical archaeology: sculpture, portraiture, sarcophagi, reliefs, architecture, architectural sculpture, topography, painting, mosaics, terracotta, gold and silver, inscriptions, numismatics, prehistory and early history. Within these categories, there are subdivisions according to typological or chronological criteria. At the same time, the objects depicted are arranged topographically. The photographs are accessible as original prints according to these classification criteria. In addition, those photographs for which the Institute holds the publication rights are indexed in so-called negative albums. Here, you can quickly see which pieces or views can be ordered as prints from the photo library. A third way to access the monuments located on Italian soil is via the so-called ‘Italy boxes’, which are arranged alphabetically by city.
Unlike other photo collections, which focus primarily on historical photographs or manage specific estates, the institute's photo library is a working tool that is constantly being expanded. The photo campaigns, carried out by our own specialist staff and in our own photo laboratory, are made possible above all by the cooperation of the antiquities authorities of the host country. Today, the focus is on supplementing the collection with regular new acquisitions, documenting new discoveries and photographing changes to museum displays of well-known works of art for scientific research purposes.
The entire photo library collection can be searched via the Arachne database.

Publications
The publication of scientific research is a central task of the DAI Rome. Various forms of book publication have been developed for this purpose.
The Mitteilungen des Deutschen Archäologischen Instituts, Römische Abteilung (German Archaeological Institute, Roman Department Communications, abbreviated to Römische Mitteilungen or RM), published annually since 1886, are the direct successor to the Annali dell’Instituto di Corrispondenza Archeologica, published from 1829 to 1885. The journal is open to contributions from researchers from all over the world in German, Italian, English and French who pursue questions of classical studies with a focus on the archaeology of Italy and North Africa.
The monographic series are important organs of the professional world for the institute's field of research, with German-language publications taking precedence. The supplementary volumes of the Römische Mitteilungen (complete Mitteilungen des Deutschen Archäologischen Instituts, Römische Abteilung. Ergänzungshefte) have a strong profile in the field of works that provide exemplary material on ancient sculpture in particular. This series was discontinued in 1999 with volume 34.
The series of special publications by the German Archaeological Institute in Rome, which has been published since 1973, is also characterised by particularly high image quality. With its generous format, it is primarily used for the publication of architecture in sophisticated building surveys. The Palilia series consists of slimmer and more affordable volumes, which are particularly open to current and new issues and also seek and find current references in the form of anthologies and colloquium publications.
